During periods of continuous flood pool releases through the turbines there will be little downstream flow variation. Conversely, releases for short periods of a few hours will have a relatively small volume and significant river stage variations will extend only a short distance downstream.
1.15 Maintenance Program. Maintenance of the proposed power plant facilities would be similar to that of any hydroelectric power plant of similar capacity. Regularly scheduled inspection and monitoring would determine when the overhaul of equipment would be necessary. An annual dewatering of the penstocks and draft tubes for inspection is planned. About every 5 years there will probably be an inspection of the tailrace.
1.16 Power Marketing. The Bureau of Reclamation is the marketing agency for electric energy generated at United States Section power plants which includes the International hydroelectric plant at Falcon and the proposed plant at Amistad Dam.
1.17 With the current energy shortage, the South Texas Electric Cooperative, Inc., and the Medina Electric Cooperative, Inc. have directed a joint letter of intent that they will enter into a contract to purchase the energy generated at Amistad Dam and at Falcon Dam at a price which will liquidate the costs of the hydroelectric power related facilities at each location. These corporations are Rural Electrification Cooperatives which are entitled under existing Federal law to preference in the sale of electric energy.
Compliance with Applicable Laws and Regulations
1.18 Project Authorization. The hydroelectric power plant operations at international reservoirs on Rio Grande are based on the 1944 Water Treaty and Minutes of the International Boundary and Water Commission. A Minute is an international agreement providing specific details for a project within the principles established in the Treaty. Additionally, the United States plant at Amistad Dam is subject to Public Law 86-605, and the operation of the United States plants at Falcon and Amistad are subject, under the Senate ratification of the 1944 Treaty, to the State of Texas making determinations of uses of the United States portion of the waters.
1.19 Water Treaty of 1944. On February 3, 1944, the United States and Mexico signed a Treaty for "Utilization of Waters of the Colorado and Tijuana Rivers and of the Rio Grande." The Treaty became effective November 8, 1945. Its stated purpose is to fix and delimit the rights of the two countries with respect to the waters of the rivers, and to obtain the most complete and satisfactory utilization thereof. The Treaty pertains to the Rio Grande between Fort Quitman, Texas, located about 85 miles downstream from El Paso-Ciudad Juarez, Chihuahua, and the Gulf of Mexico. The International Boundary and Water Commission was designated to administer the Treaty. The Treaty allots the waters of the river to the two countries. The two Governments agreed in the Treaty to construct jointly, through their respective Sections of the Commission, the dams required in the main channel of the Rio Grande for the conservation, storage, and regulation of the greatest quantity of the annual flow of the river to ensure the continuance of existing uses and the development of the greatest number of feasible projects within the limits imposed by the water allotments specified.
